lead: The engine check is where a charter week is most often saved or lost. Look at the engine cold, start it yourself, test it against the lines, and write down every number that will be read again at check-out.

sections.title: Look at it cold, with a torch

blocks.p: Ask for the engine bay to be opened before anyone starts the engine, and check it yourself. A fault found now is the base's to fix; found on Wednesday, it is yours at sea.

fig.title: Engine bay, engine cold
lines: Oil: between the marks, dark, not milky
Coolant: between MIN and MAX
Belt: about 10 mm of give, no black dust
Seacock open, strainer clear
Filter bowl: clear fuel, no dark layer
Tray and saildrive well: dry

head: You find
It means
rows: Water in the oil: the base's job
Dark layer in the filter bowl
Water or dirt: drain, new element
Soot ring at the exhaust elbow
Exhaust gas leaking into the boat
A seal weeping: an answer in writing

blocks.p: The gearbox has a dipstick too. A **packed stern gland** drips once or twice a minute while the shaft turns and is greased from its cup; a dripless seal stays dry. Have the tray wiped dry, so a new leak shows.

The **raw-water seacock** stays open: close it only to clean the strainer, while cranking a reluctant engine (open it again the moment she fires), or when you leave the boat for long. The hose looping high above the engine is the **anti-siphon loop**: it stops seawater creeping into a stopped engine.

sections.title: Start it yourself and read the panel
refs: Engine will not start: battery switch
Engine will not start: stop handle
Engine will not start: cranking and raw water
Water in the engine after a swell

blocks.p: Lever in **neutral**, key on, wait for the glow-plug light to go out, then crank. At key-on the oil and charge lamps and the buzzer come on: a lamp test. They go out seconds after the engine fires.

lines: Lamps and buzzer at key-on: a lamp test
Oil alarm still on 15 s after start: stop

blocks.p: Then look aft for **water at the exhaust**. None means no cooling: stop at once, then check seacock, strainer and impeller. A battery light that stays on means no charge: belt or alternator. An alarm blamed on a 'faulty sender' is no alarm; do not sign for it.
A diesel stops when its fuel is cut, by a stop button or pull handle; the key goes off afterwards. Push the handle back in.

fig.title: It will not start
lines: Panel dark: the engine battery switch
Cranks, no fire: stop handle left out
Many tries: close the raw-water seacock,
each crank pumps water into the exhaust
Half a turn, then solid: water inside.
Do not crank again, call the base

sections.title: Test ahead and astern with the lines on

blocks.p: Still tied up, click ahead, then astern, at idle: the boat should pull against her lines both ways. A **folding propeller** that revs without pulling is stuck half-open: neutral, a burst astern, try again. Neutral needs a click you can feel, and the engine should start only there.

blocks.rule: Gear at idle only: idle, pause in neutral, click, then throttle.

blocks.p: Test the **bow thruster** in short bursts each way. It is built for seconds: held for half a minute, its thermal cut-out trips until it has cooled and its breaker is reset.

lines: Flat water, day one: note revs and speed
Later, same revs, less speed: fouled prop

blocks.p: Check her speed at cruising revs in flat water on day one. Wind and chop take a knot or two; less speed in flat water, or black smoke at high revs, means an overloaded engine: ease back and have the propeller looked at.

sections.title: See it full, mark the filler, count the hours
refs: Fuel: range later in the week

blocks.p: 'Full on handover, full on return' works only if you saw it full: a dip, a sight glass or the fuel quay. Gauges read in quarters and stick, so count **engine hours** times the hourly burn the base gives you.

fig.title: Fuel plan for the week
lines: Tank 160 L, keep 20 L: 140 L to use
Burn at cruising revs: about 4 L/h
140 ÷ 4 = 35 hours of motoring
Plan: 6 h a day × 6 days = 36 h = 144 L
So: a fuel stop midweek

blocks.rule: Gauge and hours disagree: plan on the worse one. The reserve is not for planning.

list: Deck fillers: smell, then mark the diesel cap with tape.
Fuel quay: a slow flow, stop at the first gurgle.
Fuel shut-off: along the pipe is open, across is closed. The whole crew sees it: in an engine fire it is closed.
Petrol lives on deck, never below: its vapour sinks into the bilge.

blocks.p: An engine that surges and dies in a seaway has a blocked filter: rough water stirs a dirty tank. Sail or anchor, drain the bowl, fit a spare element, call the base.

sections.title: You sign for what you were shown

blocks.p: The engine hours on the form are what the week is measured against. Write what the panel shows and photograph it.

lines: Form says 2,290: have it corrected
Photograph the panel before you sign

list: Meter not counting: write it on the form, with how the base will charge instead.
A clause limiting engine hours: get its meaning in writing.
Not shown, like the propeller of a boat afloat: write 'not seen'.
Catamaran: both engines opened, both hours noted. A generator is a third engine, with its own seacock, strainer and hours.

blocks.p: Spares are useless without tools. Ask for a spare **impeller** and its puller, hose clips and the engine manual, and have the inventory corrected to what is aboard.
Each morning: oil, coolant, belt, strainer, a dry tray. Top the oil up to the upper mark, never above; tell the base about an engine that needs a litre a day.

lines: Buzzer, steam at the exhaust
Throttle back, neutral, stop, let it cool

blocks.p: An overheat alarm means stop before the engine seizes: sail or anchor, let it cool, then check strainer, impeller and belt. On a catamaran, stop the hot engine and carry on with the other.

head: Exhaust
Meaning
rows: Normal: it clears in a minute
Overload: ease back, check the propeller
Burning oil: top up, tell the base

blocks.p: To charge at anchor, run an hour at about 1,500 rpm: hours at tick-over charge little and harm the engine.
